requirements impose, each derived from an article in docs/planning/package-sync-conformance-criteria.md.
tests/unit/test_scenario_coverage_matrix.py enforces the cross-reference both ways.

Rules:
- A row states what an ARTICLE demands. Never derive one from a test or from the code.
  A test is one implementation; it may bundle rows, set up any way, run any direction.
- Scenario ids are stable — tests cite them. Never renumber.
- Atlas is source, Nomad is target. Sections A–K are always that direction; N may reverse.

Work, in order:
1. Section "Questions the requirements do not settle" has an `A:` ruling under each of the nine
   questions. Implement each.
2. The 35 rows marked ‼: behaviour that contradicts its article, listed under "Where the tool does
   not do what the requirements say". Fix code, tests and row together.
3. The 39 rows marked — and 3 marked P, per the "Gaps — what to test next" register.

Verify with all five: uv run pytest / ruff format --check . / ruff check . / basedpyright / codespell.
Commit with explicit pathspecs, never `git add -A` (the user edits the same tree). Batch related
edits into one commit per coherent unit.
I'll start by reading the two core documents and the enforcement test to understand the structure.

1 # Package sync conformance criteria 2 3 The intent stated in [Package sync — user requirements](package-sync-user-requirements.md), decomposed into individually checkable obligations so an implementation, its tests and its documentation can be verified against them one at a time. 4 5 Read that document first. It says what package sync is for and why it behaves as it does, which is what makes these articles cohere; this one is a checklist and is not meant to be read end to end. 6 7 Requirement ids are `PKG-FR-*` for obligations and `PKG-NG-*` for non-goals — outcomes the system is required not to attempt. MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD and MAY carry their usual normative force. How an obligation is met — which command reads what, which file holds it, how a question is worded — is not specified here; that is the specification's job. 8 9 ## Navigation 10 11 - [Package sync — user requirements](package-sync-user-requirements.md) — the intent these articles decompose 12 - [High level requirements](high-level-requirements.md) — project vision and scope 13 - [Package sync job behaviour](../jobs/package-sync.md) — operator's guide to the same jobs 14 - [Package sync specification](../system/package-sync.md) — how these requirements are implemented 15 - [ADR-020](../adr/adr-020-declarative-package-convergence.md) — the decision record behind the model 16 17 Precedence: the user requirements state the intent. Where an article here and that document disagree, the article is wrong and is what gets fixed. Where this document and anything downstream of it — the specification, the job guide, the code, the tests — disagree, this document wins. Section [Where the tool does not yet meet these requirements](#where-the-tool-does-not-yet-meet-these-requirements) records requirements the shipped code knowingly does not meet. 18 19 Every article decomposes exactly one section of the user requirements. Each section below names the section it comes from, and [Traceability](#traceability) lists the whole mapping. 20 21 ## Scope 22 23 Decomposes [What package sync is for](package-sync-user-requirements.md#what-package-sync-is-for). 24 25 The package jobs — `apt_sync`, `snap_sync`, `flatpak_sync`, `manual_installs_sync` — replicate what software is installed. Application data is not theirs. 26 27 - **PKG-FR-OPT-IN**: Every package job MUST ship disabled and MUST be enabled individually in configuration. 28 Why: enabling one authorises the system to install and remove software on the target. 29 - **PKG-FR-JOB-INDEPENDENCE**: Each package sync job MUST be enableable, reviewable and failable on its own. Enabling one MUST NOT enable another, and no job's behaviour may depend on whether another is enabled. 30 - **PKG-FR-JOB-ORDER**: All four package jobs — the three package managers and the job for software none of them can reproduce — MUST run before `folder_sync`, and the system MUST refuse to start when they are ordered otherwise. 31 Why: software must exist before data lands on top of it, or an installer's stock defaults overwrite the synced configuration. Software installed by a snippet writes those defaults exactly as a package does. 32 - **PKG-FR-APT-SCOPE**: `apt_sync` MUST cover the manually-installed apt package set, the repositories and pins that govern where those packages come from, apt's own behavioural configuration, and apt holds. Packages apt installed automatically to satisfy dependencies MUST NOT be items. 33 - **PKG-FR-SNAP-SCOPE**: `snap_sync` MUST cover installed snaps with their revision, tracking channel, confinement mode and per-snap refresh holds. 34 - **PKG-FR-FLATPAK-SCOPE**: `flatpak_sync` MUST cover installed flatpak applications per flatpak installation scope, the remotes those applications need, and mask patterns per scope. 35 - **PKG-FR-MANUAL-SCOPE**: `manual_installs_sync` MUST cover what no package manager can reproduce — apt packages whose installed version comes from no repository the machine has configured, and software under `/usr/local` and `/opt` that no package owns, found by a scan that MUST stay shallow enough to name findings rather than walk either tree — together with the registry of install snippets that is the only way such software can be reproduced on the other machine. 36 - **PKG-FR-DEB-OWNERSHIP**: Software installed from a hand-downloaded `.deb` MUST belong to `manual_installs_sync` alone. `apt_sync` MUST NOT produce an item, a review line or an install for it in any configuration. 37 Why: the target's apt has never heard the name; an apt item for it could only fail. 38 - **PKG-FR-DATA-BOUNDARY**: No package job may sync application data. Data belongs to `folder_sync`. 39 40 ## Convergence model 41 42 Decomposes [The model](package-sync-user-requirements.md#the-model). 43 44 - **PKG-FR-SOURCE-INTENT**: The source machine's state MUST be the only statement of intent, and the target MUST NOT decide anything: it answers read-only questions while the change is planned and carries out what was approved. A sync MUST NOT change what software the source has, nor where it gets it from. The writes a sync does make on the source are exactly three, each required by an article of its own: a machine-specific mark, where the source is the holding machine (`PKG-FR-MACHINE-SPECIFIC`); a snippet the review authored (`PKG-FR-MANUAL-SAME-RUN`); and the snap refresh pause, which both machines take (`PKG-FR-SNAP-REFRESH-PAUSE`). All three are covered by `PKG-FR-CONFIRM-EACH`. 45 Why: the guarantee is about software and its origins, not about the tool's own records — so the three exceptions are named here rather than left to be inferred from the articles that require them. 46 - **PKG-FR-MANAGER-CONVERGES**: Software MUST be replicated by having the target's own package managers install and remove it. The system MUST NOT copy a package manager's database, store or unpacked files between machines. What is synced is the decision, plus the configuration a manager needs in order to obey it. 47 - **PKG-FR-APT-IDENTITY**: An apt package MUST be identified by name and origin together. The system MUST NOT satisfy an approved install from an origin the source does not use. 48 Why: `gh` from a project's own repository and `gh` from the distribution archive are one name and two different pieces of software. 49 - **PKG-FR-DISTRO-ORIGIN**: All origins a machine's distribution source files declare MUST count as one origin, computed per machine. 50 Why: two machines on different mirrors are not two different origins and must not disagree about every package. 51 - **PKG-FR-SNAP-IDENTITY**: A snap MUST be identified by name alone, and the system MUST NOT ask the user anything about where a snap comes from. 52 Why: one store, and a name resolves to one publisher through an assertion snapd validates itself, so no second build of a name exists to install by mistake. 53 - **PKG-FR-FLATPAK-IDENTITY**: A flatpak application MUST be identified by its installation scope and its full reference including branch. The same application in two scopes, or on two branches, MUST be treated as two independent items — one install and one removal — and the system MUST NOT normalise the difference away. 54 Why: two branches of one application can be installed side by side, and the two scopes are configured separately. 55 - **PKG-FR-FLATPAK-ORIGIN-NOT-IDENTITY**: A flatpak application's origin remote MUST NOT be part of its identity. 56 - **PKG-FR-VERSION-FLOAT**: For apt and flatpak the system MUST install by name and accept whatever the target's own repositories offer. A version difference MUST be reported and MUST NOT be forced, upgraded or downgraded. 57 - **PKG-FR-SNAP-REVISION**: For snap the system MUST converge the target to the source's exact revision and tracking channel. 58 Why: snap keeps per-user data in revision-numbered directories, so `folder_sync` is only correct when both machines are on the same revision. 59 - **PKG-FR-BLOCKS-REPLICATE**: An apt hold, a snap refresh hold and a flatpak mask MUST each replicate as an item decided separately from the software it applies to. 60 61 ## Consent 62 63 Decomposes [The model](package-sync-user-requirements.md#the-model); the review mechanics it constrains are in [What happens during a sync](package-sync-user-requirements.md#what-happens-during-a-sync) and [Decisions and their memory](package-sync-user-requirements.md#decisions-and-their-memory-machine-specific). 64 65 - **PKG-FR-REVIEW-FIRST**: A job MUST NOT modify the target before the user has approved the changes that job proposes. 66 - **PKG-FR-ONLY-APPROVED**: A job MUST apply only what the user approved. 67 - **PKG-FR-BATCHED**: A job's questions MUST come one after another with no work between them. Where the same kind of decision recurs, the items MUST be presented together and be settleable in a single pass; a question that must show the user something before it can be answered MAY be asked on its own. Where `PKG-FR-ASK-AGAIN` permits a job to ask again, that round MUST be batched the same way: the rule binds within a round, not across a run. 68 Why: what interrupts the user is work resuming between questions, not their number. Batching constrains when a question is asked, not what shape it takes. 69 - **PKG-FR-ASK-AGAIN**: A job MAY ask again, including after it has begun changing the target, where the answer it needs rests on facts this run's own changes invalidated or that could not be established before the first change. 70 Why: correctness outranks batching, and some things are knowable only once an action has landed. What this permits is a second question, never a queue of them. 71 - **PKG-FR-CONSENT-BEFORE-CHANGE**: Every consent a job needs for a change MUST be obtained before that change is made. 72 - **PKG-FR-ASK-ABOUT-SOFTWARE**: The user MUST be asked about software, and MUST NOT be asked separately about machinery whose necessity follows from an approved package: the repository a package comes from, the key that makes that repository trusted, the pin that makes that origin's build win, the remote a flatpak application is installed from. 73 Why: the test is derivability. Approving the package answers the question; asking it separately would ask for an answer the user cannot give independently of the package, and the pairing was never expressible — a repository approved without its package does nothing, a package approved without its repository cannot be installed. 74 - **PKG-FR-ASK-WHEN-NOT-DERIVABLE**: Where the answer does not follow from any approved package, the system MUST ask. Every question this requires is specified below: apt's own behavioural configuration (`PKG-FR-APTCONF`), an unattached Ubuntu Pro target (`PKG-FR-ESM-GATE`), collateral damage to software installed by hand on the target (`PKG-FR-COLLATERAL-MANUAL`), repointing an origin that machine-specific software depends on (`PKG-FR-REPO-CONFLICT`, `PKG-FR-FLATPAK-REPOINT`), deleting a repository or a pin the source does not have (`PKG-FR-REPO-DELETE`, `PKG-FR-PIN-DELETE`), a snippet registry transfer that would lose an entry (`PKG-FR-REGISTRY-CONSENT`), and how to reproduce software no manager can (`PKG-FR-MANUAL-RESOLUTION`). 75 - **PKG-FR-NAME-THE-MACHINES**: Everything the user reads at a question — its title, the item details and warnings shown with it, the question itself and its answers — MUST identify each machine by its hostname, and "source" and "target" MUST NOT appear in any of it. The per-command confirmation is such a question: it MUST name the machine in its heading, which is why the phrase describing the change need not repeat it. Two things are outside this rule: the log, where every record already carries the machine it concerns as a field of its own, and a validation failure, which ends the run before there is anything to decide. 76 Why: source and target are roles this run assigns, not names of the user's computers. A line saying "the target loses this package" makes the reader work out which machine that is before they can answer, and the whole point of the question is which of their two machines is affected. 77 - **PKG-FR-EFFECT-NOT-MECHANISM**: Every answer offered MUST state its own effect on a named machine rather than the mechanism that produces it, and every question MUST state what the change would do before it is answered. The decisions' own names — apply, skip once, skip always — MUST NOT be the words the user reads: an answer MUST be offered as the act it performs, and MUST carry a sentence of its own naming the machine that act happens to and how long the answer lasts, a permanent one saying it will not be asked again. 78 - **PKG-FR-ANSWERS-AS-A-SET**: The answers to one question MUST read as a set: one grammar across all of them, and the machine named in every answer's sentence or in none. 79 Why: a machine named inside one answer, beside answers that name none, reads as though those answers were about something else. 80 Why: the user is deciding about their machines, not operating the tool's internals. An answer labelled with the name of an internal concept asks them to translate before they can choose. 81 - **PKG-FR-REMOVAL-DISTINCT**: Approving the removal of software MUST require a gesture distinct from approving installs, MUST NOT be the default, and MUST be presented so that the user is told the approval deletes something. 82 - **PKG-FR-SKIP-ONCE**: The user MUST be able to decline any reviewed item for the current run only. Nothing MUST be recorded, and the item MUST be offered again on the next sync. 83 - **PKG-FR-MACHINE-SPECIFIC**: The user MUST be able to mark a reviewed item as specific to one machine. A marked item MUST NOT be synced to any other machine, MUST NOT be removed or overwritten by a sync from any other machine, and MUST NOT be proposed in any later review: it is protected from every action the tool takes of its own accord. Where an approved change would touch it regardless, the user MUST be asked (`PKG-FR-COLLATERAL-MARKED`). The mark MUST be recorded on the HOLDING MACHINE and MUST NOT be synced. 84 Why: the holding machine is the one whose state the mark describes, and it is frequently not the machine the sync was launched from. Recording it anywhere else would leave the mark on a machine the item is not on. 85 - **PKG-FR-NO-MARK-ON-ORIGIN**: An apt repository and an apt pin MUST NOT be markable machine-specific, whether they are being deleted or overwritten. Declining either MUST record nothing. A flatpak remote is never a review item (`PKG-FR-FLATPAK-REMOTE-DELETE`), so there is nothing to mark. 86 Why: a mark would silence a real disagreement between the two machines about where software comes from, permanently and without further mention. Leaving them unmarkable makes that disagreement surface on every run until the user aligns the two machines. 87 - **PKG-FR-NO-MARK-ON-REPORT**: A report-only finding MUST NOT be markable machine-specific. 88 Why: no machine holds a version difference, so there is no holding machine to record it on, and a mark would stop the package syncing rather than stop the report. 89 - **PKG-FR-ABORT**: The user MUST be able to abort the whole sync at any question, and an abort MUST NOT be read as declining a single item. 90 - **PKG-FR-CONFIRM-EACH**: Every modification a package job makes MUST be covered by pc-switcher's per-command confirmation, including the decision records, the snippet registry and the snap refresh pause. No write a package job makes may bypass it. 91 Why: those three are writes the review never showed as items, so without this they would be the only changes a run makes that the user cannot see coming. 92 93 ## Preconditions and defaults 94 95 Decomposes the validation and review paragraphs of [What happens during a sync](package-sync-user-requirements.md#what-happens-during-a-sync). 96 97 - **PKG-FR-SUDO-PRECONDITION**: Each package job MUST establish in the validation step that it has passwordless sudo wherever it needs it, and MUST fail validation naming the machine that lacks it rather than degrading. What each needs: 98 99 | | source | target | 100 | - | - | - | 101 | `apt_sync` | required | required | 102 | `snap_sync` | required | required | 103 | `flatpak_sync` | none | only where a system-scope item exists on either machine | 104 | `manual_installs_sync` | none | none | 105 106 Why: it decides whether the job can run at all, so the user must learn it before the run starts changing things. Degrading is not an option for the source side of apt: without it the `/etc/apt` capture returns empty digests and the run reports success having replicated no repository configuration. 107 - **PKG-FR-APT-DPKG-LOCK**: `apt_sync` MUST refuse to start while the target's dpkg lock is held, and MUST NOT wait on it silently. 108 Why: another package operation is already changing the machine this run is about to change, so a review answered against that machine's state would be answered against state something else is moving. 109 - **PKG-FR-HARMLESS-DEFAULT**: Every reviewed item's default answer MUST be the action that does no harm — apply for an install, skip for anything that removes or overwrites. 110 Why: `PKG-FR-REMOVAL-DISTINCT` covers removals only. Overwriting a configuration file the target holds is equally irreversible and equally must not be the answer a user gets by not choosing. 111 112 ## apt 113 114 ### Installing 115 116 Decomposes [apt / Installing](package-sync-user-requirements.md#installing). 117 118 ```mermaid 119 flowchart TD 120 A["On the source,
absent on the target"] --> B{"Origin of the
source's copy"} 121 B -->|"the distribution"| C["MUST offer an ordinary install"] 122 B -->|"elsewhere"| D{"Target already offers it
from that origin?"} 123 D -->|yes| C 124 D -->|no| E{"Can the source's origin
be replicated?"} 125 E -->|yes| F["MUST offer the install,
naming the origin;
MUST provision the origin
as a consequence"] 126 E -->|no| G["MUST report the package
with origin and reason;
MUST NOT install"] 127 F --> H{"Target's real candidate
after convergence"} 128 H -->|"the source's origin"| I["MUST install"] 129 H -->|otherwise| J["MUST refuse that install,
naming both origins;
MUST continue the run"] 130 ``` 131 132 - **PKG-FR-APT-ORIGIN-DISCLOSURE**: When an approved install would come from anything other than the distribution, the user MUST be told which origin it comes from before approving it. 133 - **PKG-FR-APT-ORIGIN-DERIVED**: Approving a package MUST carry the repository, key and pins its origin needs, without a separate question and without a further question once they land. 134 Why: they are derived from the approval itself, so nothing they change can invalidate the answer that produced them. 135 - **PKG-FR-APT-ORIGIN-UNREPLICABLE**: Where no repository the source has declares the package's origin, or every repository that declares it names a key the source does not hold, the system MUST report the package with its origin and the reason, MUST NOT install it, and MUST NOT substitute another origin's build. 136 - **PKG-FR-APT-ORIGIN-VERIFY**: After repository convergence and before the first install, the system MUST verify against the target's own real state that each approved install whose origin on the source is not the distribution's own will come from the source's origin. An install that would not MUST be refused as its own failure naming both origins, and the rest of the run MUST continue. 137 Why: this check is the guarantee that `PKG-FR-APT-IDENTITY` holds; everything before it is preparation. It is not redundant with planning — a repository can fail to write, a pin can fail to win, and a distribution epoch can outrank every version an external repository publishes. The distribution is exempt because `PKG-FR-DISTRO-ORIGIN` computes it per machine: without the exemption two machines on different mirrors would fail every package. 138 139 ### Removing and diverging 140 141 Decomposes [apt / Removing a package](package-sync-user-requirements.md#removing-a-package) and [apt / Reporting without acting](package-sync-user-requirements.md#reporting-without-acting). 142 143 - **PKG-FR-APT-REMOVE**: A package on the target that the source does not have MUST be offered for removal. Approval MUST remove the package without purging its configuration. 144 - **PKG-FR-APT-SAME**: A package present on both machines at the same version from the same origin MUST produce no item. 145 - **PKG-FR-APT-VERSION-DIFF**: A version difference MUST be reported with both versions named and MUST NOT be acted on. 146 - **PKG-FR-APT-ORIGIN-DIFF**: The same package installed from different origins on the two machines MUST be reported as an origin divergence naming both origins, MUST NOT be converged, and MUST take precedence over any version difference on that package. It MUST NOT be raised for a mirror difference. 147 Why: converging it would mean a reinstall from the other origin that the user did not ask for, and builds from two different origins share no version scale. 148 149 ### Holds 150 151 Decomposes [apt / Holds](package-sync-user-requirements.md#holds). 152 153 - **PKG-FR-APT-HOLD-ITEM**: An apt hold MUST be an item separate from the package it applies to, decided separately, both when it is added and when it is removed. 154 - **PKG-FR-APT-HELD-TARGET**: A package the target has and holds MUST NOT be proposed for install or upgrade, and MUST produce no package-level item. Its hold MUST still be an item. A hold naming a package the target does not have suppresses nothing: that package MUST be offered for install like any other. 155 Why: apt records a hold for a package that is merely absent, so such a hold is bookkeeping rather than a state to protect. Reading it as one leaves the package missing on every future run. 156 - **PKG-FR-APT-HOLD-VERSION**: Where the source holds a package the target lacks, the target MUST be given the source's exact version, not whatever its repositories currently offer. Where that version cannot be obtained on the target, the install MUST fail as its own item naming both versions, and MUST NOT fall back to another version. When the job is done, the package MUST be installed at the source's version and its hold MUST be registered. 157 Why: a hold blocks install, upgrade and removal alike (measured on Ubuntu 24.04), so it carries the intent "do not move this off the version that works" as well as "do not lose this", and apt cannot distinguish them. Everywhere else a version floats because the user expressed no preference; a hold is that preference. Installing a different version and then freezing it there is worse than ordinary drift, because nothing will move it again. 158 - **PKG-FR-APT-HOLD-INERT**: Replicating a hold MUST NOT change the package's version. A hold whose install the user declined — at the review, at a collateral question asked while planning, or at one asked after the run's first change — MUST be reported as declined, not as a failure. A hold MUST fail alone only where its package's install was approved and then failed, or where the run cannot reproduce the repository that package needs. 159 Why: a hold carries no version — it freezes whatever is installed on that machine — so what replicates is the intent to freeze. Since versions float, the two machines may end up held at different versions. And a user who declined the package declined its hold with it; calling that a failure asks them to act on their own decision. 160 161 ### Collateral damage 162 163 Decomposes [apt / Collateral damage](package-sync-user-requirements.md#collateral-damage). 164 165 - **PKG-FR-COLLATERAL-AUTO**: Collateral removals, downgrades and upgrades that touch only automatically-installed packages MUST proceed without asking, and MUST be named in the run's log. 166 Why: that is the target's apt resolving its own dependency graph. Logging it is what keeps a change nobody is asked about from being a change nobody can see. 167 - **PKG-FR-COLLATERAL-MANUAL**: An approved change MUST NOT remove, downgrade or upgrade a package that is manually installed on the target unless the user has consented to that consequence specifically. Being offered for removal is not that consent: only a removal the user APPROVED may exempt a package from this protection, and one skipped for this run, or marked machine-specific, MUST keep it. The request MUST name the affected package, say why it is protected, and say what the approved change would do to it. The user MUST be able to accept it, to keep the package — leaving the changes that cause the loss unapplied rather than failing later — or to stop the sync, and each of those three MUST state its own effect. The stopping answer MUST say how far it reaches. 168 Why: "abort" alone reads as abandoning the question. Stopping here ends the entire sync, not just the package job, and a user who cannot tell those apart cannot choose between them. The protection is also not the machine-specific mark: nobody recorded a preference, the target's own package manager reports that a person asked for the package, and saying otherwise would describe a decision the user never made. 169 - **PKG-FR-COLLATERAL-MARKED**: Where the collateral package is marked machine-specific, the question MUST say so explicitly. A mark recorded earlier in the same run MUST count. 170 Why: nothing else in any review mentions a marked package, which makes this the only line the user ever gets about it, and the mark is why the job would otherwise not be touching it at all. 171 - **PKG-FR-COLLATERAL-ATTRIBUTION**: Declining collateral MUST cancel only the approved changes whose own transaction causes it, and MUST NOT cancel any other change under review. Where the collateral is caused by a combination of changes and by no single one of them, the whole set MUST be cancelled, and the question MUST say so. A consent MUST be keyed to the consequence it was given for — the change that causes it, what that change does, and the package it happens to — so consenting to one consequence for a package MUST NOT exempt it from another. 172 Why: the review's other answers are the user's and were given about other software. A decline that reaches them is a decision the user did not make. One protected package can be the casualty of two different approved changes in one run, and agreeing to lose it once is not agreeing to lose it twice. 173 - **PKG-FR-COLLATERAL-KEEPS-MARKS**: Cancelling a change on account of declined collateral MUST NOT alter a decision the user gave for that change. A change marked machine-specific MUST still be recorded as such, and a change already declined MUST NOT be re-decided. 174 175 ### Repositories, keys and pins 176 177 Decomposes [apt / Repositories, keys and pins](package-sync-user-requirements.md#repositories-keys-and-pins). 178 179 - **PKG-FR-REPO-DERIVED**: The user MUST NOT be asked to add or change a repository. A repository MUST be written to the target only because an approved package comes from it. A repository on the source that feeds no package this run syncs MUST NOT be synced. 180 - **PKG-FR-REPO-STRANDED**: A repository this run wrote for an install the user then declined MUST NOT be removed. Where no surviving approved install needs it, the run MUST name it by URL as well as by filename and say that nothing on the target installs from it. That MUST NOT be reported as a failure or a warning, and a repository still feeding a surviving approved install MUST NOT be named. 181 Why: the write has landed, and undoing it is a change nobody approved — while saying nothing leaves configuration the run added for a package that never arrived. It is not a failure: every item the user decided about ended as they decided. 182 - **PKG-FR-REPO-OVERWRITE**: A repository present on both machines with differing content MUST be overwritten with the source's version, except as required by `PKG-FR-REPO-CONFLICT`. 183 - **PKG-FR-REPO-CONFLICT**: Where overwriting would repoint a repository that software the target marked machine-specific depends on, the system MUST obtain consent first, MUST show both machines' versions of the configuration in full, and MUST NOT record the answer. Declining MUST fail every approved package whose origin depended on it, naming them, rather than installing them from elsewhere. The question MUST be raised only for a repository this run writes because an approved package comes from it. 184 Why: machine-specific software produces no review line in any run, so nothing else would tell the user its origin was about to move. Ordinary target-only software already has a removal line of its own. A differing file no approved package needs is not written at all (`PKG-FR-REPO-DERIVED`), so there is nothing to consent to — which is what makes this symmetric with `PKG-FR-FLATPAK-REPOINT`. 185 - **PKG-FR-REPO-DELETE**: A repository present on the target and not on the source MUST NOT be deleted while anything on the target still uses it — counted after this run's approved removals and counting packages the target marked machine-specific — and while that holds it MUST NOT be raised as an item at all. Once nothing uses it, its deletion MUST NOT proceed without explicit approval, and the request MUST name the repository URLs the file declares. 186 Why: the packages are the software and the repository is plumbing, so removing the packages is the decision and the repository follows. Machine-specific packages are invisible in the review by design, so a repository feeding one must never become deletable out from under it. The filename alone is not the decision: it is whatever created the file happened to call it, and two machines routinely name the same repository differently, while the URL is what the deletion actually takes away. 187 - **PKG-FR-DISTRO-FILES**: The distribution's own source files MUST be written when the target lacks them and overwritten when they differ. They MUST NEVER be removed and MUST NEVER be offered for removal. 188 Why: they are what defines "the distribution's own origin" on each machine, which is what makes `PKG-FR-DISTRO-ORIGIN` computable. 189 - **PKG-FR-APT-IGNORES**: Files apt itself does not read MUST NOT be treated as repository configuration, in any of add, change or remove. 190 - **PKG-FR-KEY-NOT-ITEM**: A signing key MUST NOT be a review item, whether it is being added, refreshed or deleted. 191 - **PKG-FR-KEY-COPY**: A key the target lacks MUST be copied byte-for-byte from the source before the repository that names it is written, whatever owns it on the source. Keys MUST NEVER be fetched over the network; they are only ever synced from the source machine. 192 Why: some projects ship packages carrying both the repository entry and its key; refusing to copy a package-owned key would make such a repository permanently untrustable. 193 - **PKG-FR-KEY-REFRESH**: A key the target holds with different content MUST be refreshed, except where the target's own distribution packaging owns it, which MUST be left alone. A key that already matches MUST NOT be touched. 194 Why: refreshing is what makes a key rotation follow the user even though rotation changes no repository file. Replacing a distribution keyring is not a sync's job. 195 - **PKG-FR-KEY-CLEANUP**: When the user approves deleting a repository, a repository-specific key that nothing on the target references any more MAY be deleted with it. A key the source still holds MUST NOT be deleted, and keys in the locations that hold ambient or distribution-owned trust MUST NEVER be deleted. 196 - **PKG-FR-PIN-ALWAYS**: Every pin the source has MUST be replicated to the target, always and without review. 197 Why: a pin is what makes an origin's build win, in the same sense a key is what makes a repository trusted, and a pin naming an origin the target does not have does nothing at all — so replicating them all costs nothing and cannot get a per-package derivation wrong. 198 - **PKG-FR-PIN-DELETE**: A pin present on the target and not the source MUST NOT be deleted without explicit approval, and the request MUST show the file's content in full. 199 Why: it is holding one origin above another on a machine the source knows nothing about, and removing it can flip which origin supplies a package at the target's next upgrade. A pin filename names neither the origin it favours nor the priority it gives it, so the file itself is the only thing the decision can rest on — and `PKG-FR-PIN-NOT-INVENTORY` rules out summarising it. 200 - **PKG-FR-PIN-NOT-INVENTORY**: A pin MUST NOT be read as a statement about the packages it names. 201 Why: a machine-wide pin would otherwise report every package on the machine, and would make a target-only package impossible to remove and impossible to silence. 202 - **PKG-FR-APTCONF**: apt's own behavioural configuration — the settings that govern how apt behaves rather than where packages come from — MUST be reviewed whether it is being added, changed or removed, with the ordinary decision and the permanent machine-specific mark. 203 Why: no approved package implies whether such a setting should be synced, so the only honest source of that answer is the user, and it is the kind of standing preference someone genuinely holds per machine. 204 205 ### Ubuntu Pro and ESM 206 207 Decomposes [apt / Ubuntu Pro](package-sync-user-requirements.md#esm-repositories--ubuntu-pro). 208 209 - **PKG-FR-ESM-GATE**: Where the source carries ESM repositories that would be written to a target reporting no Ubuntu Pro attachment, the system MUST obtain the user's decision before writing anything and before asking that job's other questions, with exactly two outcomes: attach the target, or skip the apt job for this run while the other jobs proceed. The user MUST be told what to do on the target to attach it. 210 Why: an unattached target's metadata refresh succeeds because the ESM indexes are public, so the ESM suites enter candidate selection above the ordinary archive and the failure lands later, at install time, on a package the user will not connect to the sync. The system cannot fix this itself: attaching needs a subscription token or an interactive browser flow, the source's own credentials are root-only and not reusable, and carrying a token would put a secret on a command line. 211 Measured, on an attached Ubuntu 24.04 desktop with `esm-apps` and `esm-infra` enabled: 60 of 2297 installed packages resolve their candidate to `esm.ubuntu.com`, among them `ffmpeg`, `gimp`, `imagemagick` and the `libav*` set. The earlier container measurement of zero was an artefact of a container's package set. 212 - **PKG-FR-ESM-VERIFY**: An answer claiming the target is attached MUST be verified against the target rather than believed, and the user MAY answer it any number of times. 213 - **PKG-FR-ESM-SKIP-WHOLE-JOB**: Skipping MUST leave the target's apt configuration exactly as it was found, and MUST skip the whole apt job rather than only the ESM repositories. 214 Why: pins are always synced (`PKG-FR-PIN-ALWAYS`), so the source's ESM pins would reach a target without the sources they name, leaving a candidate selection matching neither machine. An untouched configuration is a state the user can reason about. 215 - **PKG-FR-ESM-NO-ASK**: A non-interactive run MUST take the skip and MUST say why. A dry run MUST NOT ask, and MUST warn that a real run would skip the apt job. 216 Why: a dry run must not send the user off to attach a machine. 217 - **PKG-FR-ESM-PRIVACY**: Only whether the target is attached may be logged or shown. Nothing else the attachment check learns, including the subscriber's identity, may leave it. 218 219 ### Applying 220 221 Decomposes [apt / Applying apt's changes](package-sync-user-requirements.md#applying-apts-changes). 222 223 - **PKG-FR-APT-CONFIG-ATOMIC**: All repository-configuration changes a run makes MUST be applied as one unit, backed up beforehand, and followed by a single metadata refresh. If that refresh fails, every file the unit touched MUST be restored. Every approved package whose origin depended on the unit MUST then fail, named, and the run MUST continue with the packages that did not. 224 - **PKG-FR-DERIVED-FAILURE**: A derived write has no item of its own to fail; its failure MUST be charged to every approved package that needed it, naming what failed. Every such package MUST fail, including ones that would otherwise have installed. A package's own failure MUST NOT be charged back to the derived write, nor to the other packages that needed the same one. 225 Why: the user decided about a package, not about a file. 226 - **PKG-FR-DERIVED-VISIBLE**: Every derived write MUST be logged as it lands and MUST appear in a dry run's preview. 227 Why: not asking is not the same as hiding. 228 229 ## snap 230 231 Decomposes [snap](package-sync-user-requirements.md#snap). 232 233 - **PKG-FR-SNAP-CASES**: A snap on the source only MUST be offered for install at the source's revision and channel; a snap on the target only MUST be offered for removal; a difference of revision or channel MUST be offered as a single change naming both values; identical revision and channel MUST produce no item. 234 - **PKG-FR-SNAP-CONFINEMENT**: A snap's confinement mode MUST be captured on the source and replicated with the install. 235 - **PKG-FR-SNAP-REMOVE-SNAPSHOT**: Removing a snap MUST leave snapd's own pre-removal snapshot in place. 236 - **PKG-FR-SNAP-SIDELOAD**: Sideloaded snaps are out of scope (#221) and MUST be ignored on both machines: never installed, never removed, never offered as an item, and never the subject of a hold item. A run MUST name the ones it found so the user knows they are unmanaged, and MUST do nothing else about them. 237 Why: no store can serve such a revision and nothing carries the file between machines, so a snap the tool cannot reinstall must not be one it offers to delete. Handling half of the case, and later handling the other half from a different job, is worse than leaving it alone until the whole case is designed. 238 - **PKG-FR-SNAP-FAIL-ITEM**: A snap whose revision the target cannot fetch MUST fail as its own item, and the rest of the run MUST continue. 239 - **PKG-FR-SNAP-HOLD**: A snap refresh hold MUST be an item of its own, both when it is added and when it is removed. A hold recorded for a snap the source no longer has MUST produce no item, and no command a sync issues may set a standing hold as a side effect. 240 - **PKG-FR-SNAP-REFRESH-PAUSE**: Automatic snap refreshes MUST be suspended on both machines for the duration of a run and MUST NOT interfere with the run's own revision convergence. Each machine's prior refresh policy MUST be restored afterwards, including an indefinite hold the user set. Where the prior policy cannot be read on a machine, that machine's policy MUST be left untouched. Where the suspension cannot be set or cannot be confirmed, the run MUST say so and MUST continue with that machine unsuspended rather than failing. The suspension MUST expire by itself, so a run that dies without cleaning up MUST NOT leave a machine's automatic refreshes suspended. 241 Why: snapd refreshes several times a day and would otherwise move a revision mid-sync. It is a guard against a race, not a precondition: refusing to sync because the guard could not be set costs the user more than the race it prevents. 242 - **PKG-FR-SNAP-DATA-BOUNDARY**: Data directories of revisions the target's snapd never installed MUST NOT be synced. 243 Why: they would leave orphan data behind on the target. 244 245 ## flatpak 246 247 Decomposes [flatpak](package-sync-user-requirements.md#flatpak). 248 249 - **PKG-FR-FLATPAK-CASES**: An application on the source only MUST be offered for install; on the target only, for removal; the same application, scope and branch at different versions MUST be reported only; identical MUST produce no item. 250 - **PKG-FR-FLATPAK-REMOTE-DERIVED**: A remote MUST NOT be a review item when it is added or changed. It MUST be synced because an application approved this run comes from it, including the remote that supplies an approved application's runtime, and declining the application MUST be the only way to decline the remote. A remote that feeds no application approved this run MUST NOT be synced, and no remote is exempt from this rule. 251 Why: a fresh flatpak installation configures zero remotes, so there is no "distribution" remote the way apt has a distribution archive. 252 - **PKG-FR-FLATPAK-REMOTE-FIRST**: Every derived remote MUST be provisioned before the first application installs. 253 - **PKG-FR-FLATPAK-REMOTE-TRUST**: A remote MUST replicate with its trust, not only its name and URL: whether the source verifies its signatures and, where it does, its signing key, copied byte-for-byte and never fetched over the network. Where the source's trust rests on a machine-level anchor rather than a key of the remote's own, that anchor MUST be copied the same way. A verified remote MUST NOT be replicated as an unverified one; a remote the source itself does not verify MUST be replicated unverified and the user MUST be told. Where the source verifies a remote and holds no key material for it anywhere, the remote MUST be replicated as the source has it, with a warning, and MUST NOT fail the applications that need it. 254 Why: without the key a replicated remote is configured but unusable and every install from it fails. The last case is not that: installs from such a remote already fail on the source, so refusing them on the target would report a target failure for a source condition. 255 - **PKG-FR-FLATPAK-REPOINT**: A remote present on both machines whose URL, verification setting or key differs MUST be repointed in place without a review line and without disturbing the applications that name it as their origin — except where the repoint would move the origin of an application the target marked machine-specific, in which case the system MUST obtain consent first, MUST show both configurations, MUST name the applications that are the reason, and MUST NOT record the answer. Declining MUST fail every approved application that needed the source's URL, citing the decision. A difference of key alone MUST NOT raise the question. 256 Why: importing a key can neither move an application's origin nor withdraw trust, since flatpak merges imported keys rather than replacing them. 257 - **PKG-FR-FLATPAK-REMOTE-DELETE**: A remote MUST NOT be a review item, whether it is being added, changed or deleted. A remote the source does not have MUST be deleted once nothing on the target still uses it, counted after this run's approved removals against what the machine actually has — including applications the target marked machine-specific and applications reported as an origin divergence. While anything still uses it, it MUST NOT be deleted. Deleting a remote MUST take its signing key with it. 258 Why: the applications are the software and the remote is plumbing, so removing the applications is the decision and the remote follows. Asking separately let the user delete a remote whose applications are invisible to the review — a machine-specific one, or one reported as an origin divergence — and strand them. 259 - **PKG-FR-FLATPAK-INSTALL-ORIGIN**: An application MUST be installed from the source's remote or not at all, and the source's remote MUST be identified by its URL and verification setting rather than its name. The system MUST verify this against the target's own state before the install and MUST verify the landed origin after it; either failure MUST fail that application alone, naming both URLs. 260 Why: two remotes can share a name and serve different builds of the same application, with success reported either way, and re-adding an existing remote name succeeds without changing where it points — so neither a matching name nor a successful add is evidence. 261 - **PKG-FR-FLATPAK-MISSING-REMOTE**: An application whose origin remote exists neither on the target nor among this run's own additions MUST be refused as its own item naming the missing remote. 262 - **PKG-FR-FLATPAK-ORIGIN-DIFF**: The same application, scope and branch installed from different remotes on the two machines MUST be reported as an origin divergence naming both remotes and both URLs, MUST NOT be converged, and MUST take precedence over a version difference on that application. Origins MUST be compared by URL, never by remote name. 263 Why: flatpak refuses to install a reference already installed from another remote, so the only mechanical convergence would be uninstalling what the user has and reinstalling it from the other origin. 264 - **PKG-FR-FLATPAK-REMOTE-FAILURE**: A remote that cannot be provisioned has no item of its own to fail; the failure MUST land on every application that needed it, naming the remote and quoting flatpak's own error. 265 - **PKG-FR-FLATPAK-FILTER**: A remote the source restricts with a filter MUST be replicated with that filter. The filter file MUST be copied byte-for-byte from the source to the same absolute path on the target and re-applied to the replicated remote. It is derived like a signing key and MUST NOT be a review item. No filter may be in force on a remote this run provisions while the approved applications from that remote install, whichever machine set it, and a remote the source does not restrict MUST NOT stay restricted on the target. A filter that cannot be copied or re-applied MUST fail every approved application from that remote, naming the remote and the path. 266 Why: flatpak stores the filter's path rather than its content, so the content is an ordinary file the run can carry byte-for-byte exactly as it carries a signing key; replicating the remote without it silently widens what the target offers. 267 Why the ordering: a filter can be narrower than the set the source has installed, so one in force during the installs blocks the very replication it describes — the target's own as easily as the source's. Measured on Flatpak 1.14.6: installing a reference its remote's filter denies exits 1 with `Nothing matches in remote ` and lands nothing, while the same install of an allowed reference succeeds ([measurements](../adr/considerations/adr-020-flatpak-filter-and-trust-measurements.md)). 268 - **PKG-FR-FLATPAK-THIRD-SCOPE**: An installation that is neither the user nor the system one MUST be skipped. 269 - **PKG-FR-FLATPAK-MASK**: Mask patterns MUST replicate per scope, added and removed alike, whether or not anything currently matches them, and MUST land after the applications. Editing or moving a pattern MUST be reported as found and MUST NOT be normalised. 270 - **PKG-FR-FLATPAK-PRIVILEGE**: A run that touches only the user scope MUST NOT require root on the target. 271 272 ## Manual installs 273 274 Decomposes [Software no manager can reproduce](package-sync-user-requirements.md#software-no-manager-can-reproduce). 275 276 - **PKG-FR-MANUAL-RESOLUTION**: Every detected item MUST end the run in one of exactly three states: reproducible by an install snippet, marked machine-specific, or skipped for this run. Skipping for this run MUST count as a resolution, not as an unresolved state. 277 - **PKG-FR-MANUAL-SOURCE-DECIDES**: Whether an item is reproducible MUST be decided by what the source holds. An item with a snippet only on the target MUST still be treated as unresolved. 278 - **PKG-FR-MANUAL-SAME-RUN**: A snippet authored during a review MUST be persisted, transferred and replayed in the same run. 279 - **PKG-FR-SNIPPET-VERBATIM**: A snippet MUST be stored and replayed exactly as written. The system MUST NOT parse, interpret or reason about it. It MUST run as the target user with no privilege added around it, and MUST run without standing input so that a command expecting input fails rather than hanging the sync. An empty snippet MUST NOT be accepted as a resolution. 280 - **PKG-FR-REGISTRY-SYNCS**: The snippet registry MUST sync between machines. 281 Why: how to install something is knowledge about the software, not about the machine — unlike the machine-specific marks of `PKG-FR-MACHINE-SPECIFIC`, which are never synced. 282 - **PKG-FR-REGISTRY-CONSENT**: A registry transfer that would lose or change an entry the target holds MUST NOT proceed without consent, and MUST name the affected entries. Declining MUST abort the run, and a non-interactive run MUST abort. 283 Why: aborting lets the user consolidate the two registries by hand; the alternative silently drops the target's snippets. 284 - **PKG-FR-MANUAL-FAIL-ITEM**: A snippet that has vanished between planning and replay, or whose replay fails, MUST fail as its own item naming the item, and the run MUST continue. 285 286 ## Reporting, failure and the dry run 287 288 Decomposes [When something goes wrong](package-sync-user-requirements.md#when-something-goes-wrong) and the dry-run and no-terminal paragraphs of [What happens during a sync](package-sync-user-requirements.md#what-happens-during-a-sync). 289 290 - **PKG-FR-OUTCOME-SUCCESS**: A job MUST report success when every item it presented received an answer and the job did what those answers said — including when it presented nothing because the target already matches, and including when every answer was to decline. 291 Why: declining is an answer. A job whose review was put to the user and settled did its work, whatever the settlement was. 292 - **PKG-FR-OUTCOME-SKIPPED**: A job that could not put its review to the user, or that ended before it had one, MUST report skipped rather than success, MUST say why, MUST record no decision, MUST transfer no registry and MUST leave the target untouched. The run MUST continue and the exit code MUST be unaffected. 293 Why: skipped means nobody decided, which is what separates a run the user answered "no" to from one where the question was never put. The two cases are a run with no terminal (`PKG-FR-NO-TERMINAL`) and the apt job an unattached target ends (`PKG-FR-ESM-SKIP-WHOLE-JOB`). 294 - **PKG-FR-OUTCOME-FAILED**: A job MUST report failure when at least one approved item could not be applied. Every approved item MUST be attempted, failures MUST be collected and reported together naming each item, one failed item MUST NOT block the rest of its job, and one failed job MUST NOT stop the others. 295 - **PKG-FR-NO-TERMINAL**: A non-interactive run — one with no interactive terminal — MUST ask nothing, MUST treat every reviewable item as declined for this run, and MUST report every package job with a non-empty review as skipped. Nothing may be recorded, no snippet written and no registry transferred. A job whose review is empty has nothing to decline and reports success (`PKG-FR-OUTCOME-SUCCESS`); it still transfers no registry. 296 - **PKG-FR-DRY-RUN**: A dry run MUST produce the same plan and the same review as a real run and MUST issue no command that changes either machine. The preview MUST include the derived changes that have no review line of their own. A dry run on a terminal MUST report success; without one it MUST report skipped, for the same reason a real run does. 297 - **PKG-FR-READ-FAILS-JOB**: A read a job's findings rest on that cannot be answered at all MUST fail its own job, naming the command that did not answer, and MUST NOT stop the run's other jobs. This covers the scans a job runs itself as well as the package managers it queries. Silence MUST NOT be read as an empty installed set or an empty scan. An empty answer is ordinary data. 298 Why: reading silence as "this machine has nothing installed" would propose removing everything the other machine has, and reading a dead scan as "everything here is unowned" would ask the user to write an install snippet for every entry under it. 299 - **PKG-FR-LOG-DECISIONS**: A run's log MUST name every item a job presented together with the decision it received, and every change a package manager made on its own behalf that no review showed. 300 Why: the report says what a job did; the log is where the user reconstructs why, including the changes that were never theirs to approve. 301 - **PKG-FR-LOG-VERBATIM**: A package manager's own output MUST be kept verbatim in the debug log, subject to `PKG-FR-ESM-PRIVACY` and `PKG-FR-CREDENTIAL-PRIVACY`. 302 - **PKG-FR-CREDENTIAL-PRIVACY**: A credential embedded in a URL MUST be withheld wherever the system logs that URL or puts it in front of the user — a log line, a command trace, a package manager's output, a review item, a configuration file displayed in full for a decision, and an install snippet's body displayed for one. What is withheld is the URL's `userinfo` as RFC 3986 defines it, so no character that grammar permits may end the withholding early. This binds the display alone: what is stored and replayed stays exactly as written (`PKG-FR-SNIPPET-VERBATIM`). 303 Why: a private or commercial repository carries its credential in its own address, so the URL is the secret. A log file is readable by anyone with an account on the machine that wrote it. Redacting what is stored or replayed would instead break the install the snippet exists to reproduce. 304 - **PKG-FR-FAIL-NAMED**: Every failure MUST name the item, package or file it concerns. 305 306 ## Non-goals and accepted costs 307 308 Decomposes [What this deliberately does not do](package-sync-user-requirements.md#what-this-deliberately-does-not-do). 309 310 Each of these is a real cost, given up knowingly. 311 312 - **PKG-NG-APT-LINE-CONTROL**: The target's apt configuration is not under the user's line-by-line control. Repositories, keys and pins appear because a package was approved, and declining the package is the only way to decline them. 313 - **PKG-NG-APT-IDENTICAL**: The two machines' apt configurations are converged for what packages need, not made identical. 314 - **PKG-NG-PIN-LOCAL**: A pin cannot be kept on one machine only. It returns on every sync until it is deleted on the source. 315 - **PKG-NG-SNAP-ORIGIN**: snap has no origin model and needs none. 316 - **PKG-NG-ESM-PARTIAL**: A target with no Ubuntu Pro attachment costs the whole apt job for that run, not only the ESM repositories. 317 - **PKG-NG-MARK-ORIGIN**: Deleting an apt configuration file can be marked machine-specific; deleting an apt repository, an apt pin or a flatpak remote cannot. 318 - **PKG-NG-MANUAL-REMOVE**: Manual installs cannot be removed. The job keeps no record of what it put on the target. 319 - **PKG-NG-VERSION-CONVERGE**: Version drift is reported, never resolved, for apt and flatpak. Aligning two machines' versions is the user's job. 320 - **PKG-NG-ORIGIN-CONVERGE**: A divergence of origin is reported, never resolved, for apt packages and flatpak applications alike. Where both machines have the same software from different origins, the system will not pick one. 321 - **PKG-NG-UNATTENDED**: A package job's review cannot be answered by a non-interactive run. There is no file of standing answers and no assume-yes option. 322 - **PKG-NG-MARK-PORTABILITY**: Machine-specific marks are per manager and per machine and are deliberately never synced. A new machine means deciding again. 323 - **PKG-NG-AUTOMATION-ENV**: The environment variable `PCSWITCHER_PACKAGE_REVIEW_AUTOMATION` answers a package review from a JSON map of item id to decision, and its answers count as the user's own — a permanent one writes a machine-specific mark or an install snippet. It exists for the integration tests, which have no terminal to answer at, and MUST stay out of `--help` and the configuration schema so nothing offers it as a way of running the tool. Anything able to set it in the environment of a real run therefore gets silent, unreviewed, permanent decisions. This is the accepted cost of testing the review at all; `PKG-NG-UNATTENDED` still holds for every documented path. 324 325 ## Where the tool does not yet meet these requirements 326 327 Read against the code at `c6e4bf33`; articles untouched since `502321ec` were last read there. Below is every article not met in full, and every cost knowingly accepted in meeting one; every other article was found satisfied. Evidence is symbol names, because the code moves. 328 329 ### apt 330 331 - **PKG-FR-COLLATERAL-MANUAL** is met except inside the removal batch. `collateral.Collateral.plan_time` exempts the removal candidates from the removal simulation alone — every one of them is in that transaction by construction — so a candidate the user skips can still be carried off by another approved removal's cascade. `packages.PackageConverger.remove`'s guard refuses that transaction and names the package, so nothing is lost, but the user is told rather than asked. Closing it needs one `apt-get --dry-run` per candidate on every run with removals, which is the cost the batched simulation exists to avoid. 332 - **PKG-FR-COLLATERAL-MANUAL** can also ask about collateral the real command would never produce. lines=txt.split('\n')

    m=re.match(r'- \*\*([A-KN]\d+)\*\*', l)
    if m: reg.append(m.group(1))

# marks
marks={}
for l in lines:
    if not l.startswith('| '): continue
    c=[x.strip() for x in l.strip().strip('|').split('|')]
    if len(c)<3: continue
    if re.fullmatch(r'[A-KN]\d+', c[0]): marks[c[0]]=c[-2]
from collections import Counter
print("register entry marks:", Counter(marks.get(r,'MISSING') for r in reg))
targets=[r for r,m in marks.items() if m in ('—','P')]
print("42 targets without register entry:", [r for r in targets if r not in reg])
print("register entries marked U/UV/V:", [r for r in reg if marks.get(r) in ('U','U V','V')])
EOF

Removing a snap leaves snapd's own pre-removal snapshot in place — the only recovery path if the removal was a mistake.

### Refresh holds

Refresh holds replicate as their own items, both when added and when removed. A hold recorded for a snap the source no longer has produces no item.

### Sideloaded snaps

Snaps installed from a local `.snap` file are out of scope (#221). They are ignored on both machines: never installed, never removed, never an item. A run names the ones it found so the user knows they are unmanaged, and does nothing else about them.

## flatpak

flatpak follows the shape every job has: what the source has is offered for install, what only the target has for removal, what cannot be converged is reported. What is particular to flatpak:

### Identity

A flatpak application is identified by its **scope** and its **full reference including branch**. The same application in both scopes, or on two branches, is two independent items — one install and one removal — reported as found.

Origin is not part of that identity: flatpak refuses to install a reference already present from a different remote, so a difference of origin is reported rather than converged, and takes precedence over a version difference.

This means `folder_sync`'s exclude set has to be narrowed by what `snap_sync` actually did, so work out how that information reaches it (`PKG-FR-JOB-ORDER` puts the package jobs first, which is what makes it available) and record the mechanism in `docs/system/package-sync.md`.

2. **K81 — with `snap_sync` off, every revision's data is mirrored.** The snap filters are emitted only when `_package_job_enabled("snap_sync")` holds, which is false both when the job is disabled and when the sibling map is absent, and nothing unconditional names anything under `~/snap`. `folder_sync`'s own comment records this as a deliberate trade (D-29), so this is a conflict between a documented choice and `PKG-FR-SNAP-DATA-BOUNDARY`. Note that row K23's ruling has already settled that `folder_sync` may read the package jobs' switches — that is not the problem here; the problem is what gets mirrored when it reads them as off. Decide it against the articles: either the article gains the exception, with a *Why*, or the code stops needing one. Whichever way it goes, the ADR that records D-29 must end up agreeing with the criteria.

3. **K88 — the snippet registry is mirrored outside its own consent.** The registry lives at `~/.config/pc-switcher/package-snippets.yaml`, beside the decision files, but `folder_sync`'s non-overridable exclusion is the glob `*.decisions.yaml`, which does not match it. Wherever `~/.config` is a synced folder, `folder_sync` carries the registry Atlas→Nomad after the package jobs have run — the transfer `PKG-FR-REGISTRY-CONSENT` exists to gate, and one that `PKG-FR-OUTCOME-SKIPPED` and `PKG-FR-NO-TERMINAL` both forbid when the job was skipped. Fix the exclusion. Read `_decision_file_exclude_filters` for the shape, and mind the project rule that an rsync filter must carry no inline comment.

4. **G72 — a registry entry's authoring record is overwritten without asking.** `_guard_registry_overwrite` compares bodies alone, while a `Snippet` also carries `label`, `authored_at` and `authored_on`, all of which the whole-file transfer replaces. `PKG-FR-REGISTRY-CONSENT` gates a transfer that would "lose or change an entry the target holds". What is lost is metadata — the replayed body stays byte-identical — so the consequence is narrow; fix it so the comparison covers the whole entry, and make sure the question still reads sensibly when the only difference is an authoring record.

5. **H167 — the article overstates the automation hatch.** `PKG-NG-AUTOMATION-ENV` says a permanent answer given through the environment variable writes "a machine-specific mark **or an install snippet**". `_decisions_from_automation` returns decisions only, so `ReviewOutcome.snippets` is always empty on that path and no snippet can be authored through it. `review.py`'s own docstring already states the narrower, correct version. **Measured** on apt 2.8.3 / Ubuntu 24.04 by pointing apt at scratch directories one filename at a time (`apt-cache policy -o Dir::Etc::preferencesparts=`, `APT_CONFIG` with `Dir::Etc::parts=`, `apt-get update --print-uris -o Dir::Etc::sourceparts=`) and asking whether the file took effect; cross-checked against `man 5 apt_preferences`, `man 5 apt.conf`, `man 5 sources.list` and `apt-config dump | grep Ignore-Files-Silently`. Both say the same thing: a question whose article scopes it to *approved* work must be built after those answers exist, not from the plan-time superset. Three rows turn on it.

1. **The repository-conflict question (question "C", to be removed from "Questions the requirements do not settle").** `PKG-FR-REPO-CONFLICT`: the question "MUST be raised only for a repository this run writes because an approved package comes from it". The code raises it from the plan-time superset of *proposed* installs, so a file can be asked about and then not written. Raise it from the approvals instead.

2. **D47 (`‼`).** `PKG-FR-COLLATERAL-MARKED` requires the collateral question to say explicitly that the package is marked machine-specific, and requires a mark recorded earlier in the same run to count. The protection counts at the apply-time guard, but items — and therefore every question and every "why it is protected" sentence — are built before any answer exists, and `Collateral._reason` deliberately does not consult `_run_marked`. 3. **C172 and N12 (`‼`).** `PKG-FR-REPO-DELETE`: a repository still in use "MUST NOT be raised as an item at all", counted after this run's **approved** removals. The previous agent made the deletion not *proceed* when the removal that would free it was declined, which is as far as a plan-time count reaches — but the item is still raised in the same review as the package's removal. Its note records that closing it needs the question built after the answers, which is exactly what you are building. N12 says the repository is not raised at all when the package's removal is declined; C172 says the same for the one package that repository feeds.

## Constraints on the design

- `PKG-FR-BATCHED`: a job's questions come one after another with no work between them, and a recurring kind of decision is settled in one pass. A second round inside the review, with no executor work between, does not violate it — but read the article and `PKG-FR-ASK-AGAIN` and say in your report which one licenses what you build.
- `PKG-FR-REVIEW-FIRST` and `PKG-FR-CONSENT-BEFORE-CHANGE` still hold: nothing may be written before the whole review settles.
- The B41 ruling landed earlier today and already made one class of item depend on another item's decision (`sync_core.py`, `_blocks_riding_software`, decision propagation in `accept_review`). Read it first — the mechanism you need may already be half-built there, and the two must not fight.

Confirmed on a real Ubuntu 24.04 machine: `dpkg` owns **neither** `/usr/local/lib` (no package at all) nor `/usr/local/bin` other than incidentally, and `base-files` ships neither. So on a stock machine the scan reports its own roots as unreproducible software — asking the user to write an install snippet for a directory the FHS ships empty. That is a product defect, not a test expectation error: `PKG-FR-MANUAL-SCOPE` scopes the scan to *software under* those trees.

The run also stopped at that failure, so tests ordered after it (E53, J145 among them) never ran.

## Where the tool does not yet meet these requirements

- **PKG-FR-COLLATERAL-MANUAL** is met except inside the removal batch. `collateral.Collateral.plan_time` exempts the removal candidates from the removal simulation alone — every one of them is in that transaction by construction — so a candidate the user skips can still be carried off by another approved removal's cascade. `packages.PackageConverger.remove`'s guard refuses that transaction and names the package, so nothing is lost, but the user is told rather than asked. - **PKG-FR-COLLATERAL-MANUAL** can also ask about collateral the real command would never produce. Accepted: the question over-asks and never under-asks, which is the only way round that is safe.

**CI: integration passed — 32m39s, the full suite, including all twelve new VM tests and the G28 fix.** The lint/unit workflow is re-running after a transient `dorny/paths-filter@v4` failure that skipped both.

Now your questions.

## The snap mark bug — answering only

**Do I see a case?** Weakly. The requirements permit it: `PKG-FR-MACHINE-SPECIFIC` lets the user mark *any* reviewed item, with no exception for snap, and `PKG-FR-SNAP-CASES` makes a revision/channel difference a reviewed item. So the code has to handle it. But I can't point to a user need I'd defend — snaps auto-refresh, so pinning one machine's revision by mark is fragile. If you think nobody would ever want it, the cleaner answer is an article saying a snap revision change is not markable, and then the case disappears instead of being handled.

**Did I change anything?** Yes. `_decision_holder_is_source` became `_mark_holders`: a `CHANGE` is now target-held, and later runs read both machines' decision files.

**Current behaviour:** marking a snap revision/channel change records on Nomad, whose revision the answer keeps; later runs from either machine raise no item for that snap.

**Before:** recorded on Atlas, read per-side — so the mark dropped the snap from one manifest and left the other machine's copy unmatched, and the next run offered it for removal. One correction to how I put it earlier: that was measured on stubs, not on a machine.

## "Third drift mode" and "ratchet"

Plainly: the coverage doc and the test suite are two descriptions of the same thing, and they can disagree three ways. (1) The doc cites a test that doesn't exist. (2) The doc's gap list still names work that's been done. (3) A test exists and proves a row, but the checker can't recognise its docstring tag, so the row reads as unproven. Only (1) was caught before; (3) is the bad one because it understates coverage and looks like honest remaining work.

On the word: I didn't introduce it. It's in `tests/unit/test_scenario_coverage_matrix.py` at commit `cc7ca2c9`, before this session — *"These tests are the ratchet."* Happy to rename it throughout if you'd rather; it's your codebase's vocabulary either way.

## "Costs the criteria knowingly accept"

`docs/planning/package-sync-conformance-criteria.md` has a section **"Where the tool does not yet meet these requirements"** listing articles the shipped code knowingly doesn't meet. That's what the phrase points at. Your challenges land:

- **D37** — you're right, and so is the article: the user wants the *choice*. Being told "I refused your transaction because pkg-b would go" is strictly worse than being asked "pkg-a's removal takes pkg-b with it — accept, keep pkg-b, or stop?". The cost is one `apt-get --dry-run` per removal candidate. I'd pay it.
- **D38** — a hold on a package the target doesn't have is apt bookkeeping, and `PKG-FR-APT-HELD-TARGET` already rules it "bookkeeping rather than a state to protect" and requires the package be offered for install normally. Your "abort and tell the user to clean up" contradicts that article. One or the other has to give — that's your call, not mine to take.
- **F43** — you're half right and I should be exact. The *article* `PKG-FR-FLATPAK-REMOTE-TRUST` has no exception; the exception lives only in that shortfall section, which is not the requirement. If your ruling is "no exceptions", the fix is to read `gpgkeypath` out of the remote's ostree config and carry that key too.
- **F117** — the clear happens first because a filter can be narrower than what's being replicated, so a filter in force blocks the very apps being installed (measured, Flatpak 1.14.6). And yes: with filters off, apps the target's filter would have denied can land. So the user needs a warning naming the filter that couldn't be applied *and* saying whether anything installed that it would have restricted. A `remote-modify --filter=` failure is not realistic in normal operation — agreed we shouldn't be clever about it, we should warn.

## The `P` rows — you're right about most of them

- **D61** — agreed, not partial. Overriding a `SKIP_ONCE` to `SKIP_ONCE` is unobservable, so there is no second half. Should be `U`.
- **F121** — agreed. Covered by F119+F120, and the row's own text says third-scope remotes can't reach the listings. Whether it's *relevant*: it's a negative control against re-introducing the bug. Keep it as `U` or delete it; I lean keep.
- **H133** — same shape, covered by construction. Should be `U`.
- **J107** — describes a case that doesn't exist. It isn't a branch the requirements distinguish; I'd delete the row.
- **K67** — genuinely partial: nothing asserts no job degrades to a reduced capture. Real work.
- **K89** — trivially closable: assert `home.filter`'s `- .cache/*` covers `.cache/pc-switcher`. Should just be done.

The common thread is that "covered by construction" was used to avoid tagging existing tests. Tagging them and marking `U` is simpler and truer.

## The four Gaps entries

K67 and K89 (above), plus **K82** and **K88** — both proven at unit level with no VM test. They're honest gaps, and K82/K88 are writable now that integration is green.

## VM coverage

Yes — **nothing about collateral damage is tested on real machines at all.** The reason those four bullets exist is simply that nobody wrote the tests; there's no principled barrier. Given the suite now passes in 33 minutes, collateral and the apt origin model are the two worth writing, because both turn on what real apt does that a mock can't show.

## G28's limit of 25

I made it up — no requirement sets a limit. It should go, or be replaced by something grounded.

On scope: I agree the FHS skeleton isn't software, and `/usr/local/{etc,games,include,man,sbin,src}` are still reported today. Narrowing to `/opt/*` and `/usr/local/{bin,sbin,lib}/*` would fix that, but it changes what `PKG-FR-MANUAL-SCOPE` covers, and it would stop finding a tarball unpacked as `/usr/local/pycharm` — which is exactly the case the user requirements describe. `/usr/local/src` is where source builds land, so I'd keep it.

Before I queue that work: **do you want the scan narrowed to a fixed list of directories, or kept at `/usr/local/*` and `/opt/*` with the stock empty skeleton directories filtered out?** The second keeps `/usr/local/pycharm` findable; the first is simpler and loses it.

Root cause, and it isn't transient:

**The branch is 402 commits ahead of `main`, and `dorny/paths-filter` fetches `--deepen=400`.** The merge-base is out of reach, so the fetch dies with `shallow file has changed since we read it` and the filter job fails. The previous run passed at 401; my six commits crossed the line.

The consequence matters more than the red tick: when that job fails, **Lint and Unit Tests are skipped entirely** — yet `CI Status` still reports pass. So the PR currently shows green on the aggregate check while its unit tests have not run in CI at all. Integration is genuinely green (32m39s, real VMs); lint and unit are green only on my local runs.

Every further push to this branch will fail the same way, and it gets worse, not better, as commits accumulate.

The standard fix is one line in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — give that job's `actions/checkout@v7` a `fetch-depth: 0` so the filter has the history it needs and never has to deepen. Alternatives are bumping the deepen number (which just moves the cliff) or dropping the filter for this job.

I haven't touched it: it's shared CI configuration and you didn't ask for a workflow change. Say the word and it's a one-line commit.

One sentence was needed in the article, because the section it sits in opens "The package jobs … replicate what software is installed", so the prohibition could be read as scoped to those jobs. That reading is what licensed the gating in the first place.

**A correction to what I told you earlier.** I said that with `snap_sync` off, per-revision snap data is no longer mirrored at all. That was wrong, and two docs said it too. It travels wherever both machines are on the same revision — which is precisely what the target's own listing reports. Fixed in the docs and in what I claimed.

I would consider a hold without the package being installed (whether this situation is found on source or target) as bookkeeping failure. Tell user to fix and abort. Rare case. Simple way to protect us from difficult situation that would require much logic for very small chance we every encounter it.
So only situations:
- package not installed on target yet -> install pkg and add hold  (mention that there is a hold during package selection review)
- package to remove from target -> uninstall pkg and remove hold

Measured on this machine (Ubuntu 24.04) rather than reasoned from the FHS.

**Simpler in wording — yes. Complete — no, for two reasons.**

## 1. "The standard skeleton" is not one level deep

If the skeleton is merely *excluded*, every hand-installed binary vanishes: `/usr/local/bin` holds `talosctl`, `yq`, `flux`, `batteryhealthchargingctl-janfr`, none dpkg-owned. So the rule must descend into skeleton directories, not just skip them.

But descending re-creates the same problem one level down. Unowned by any package, on a stock-ish machine:

| Descend into | What you get |
| --- | --- |
| `bin` | `talosctl`, `yq`, `flux`, … — **genuine finds** |
| `share` | `ca-certificates`, `fonts`, `man`, `sgml`, `texmf`, `xml` — **6 stock dirs, pure noise** |
| `lib` | `python3.12` — **noise** |
| `sbin`, `games`, `src`, `etc`, `include` | empty here |

So "except the standard skeleton" is under-specified: the skeleton is a *tree*, and a flat name list only handles its first level. Left as you wrote it, you'd trade 2 noise findings for 7.

**What I'd do instead:** exclude `etc`, `include`, `man`, `share`, `lib` entirely; descend one level into `bin`, `sbin`, `games`, `src`; report every other entry under `/usr/local` (that's `/usr/local/pycharm`) and everything under `/opt`. Measured against this machine that yields exactly the hand-installed binaries and non-skeleton directories, with zero stock noise. What it gives up is a tarball that drops only into `/usr/local/lib` or `/usr/local/share` with nothing in `bin` — rare, and usually the binary is what you'd notice anyway.

## 2. "…for which we have the repo" double-reports

That qualifier is doing work you already get for free, and it costs you a duplicate. Since this morning's G5 fix, the package half of the scan reads the source's *installed* set, so **any package whose version comes from no configured repository is already a finding by name**. Add your qualifier and a hand-`.deb` gets reported twice — once as `code`, once as `/opt/code`.

Measured examples of paths that are dpkg-owned here: `/opt/google` (google-chrome-stable), `/opt/az` (azure-cli), `/opt/Falco` (falco-app), `/usr/local/Brother` (brscan3). Whether those packages have a repo is exactly the question the *other* half answers.

So the path exclusion should be plain: **owned by any package dpkg knows about**.

## The rule I'd write

> A finding is any entry under `/opt`, under `/usr/local`, or one level inside `/usr/local/{bin,sbin,games,src}`, that no dpkg package owns. `/usr/local/{etc,include,man,share,lib}` are the distribution's own skeleton and are never findings, nor scanned.

Two notes: `/usr/local/man` is a symlink to `share/man` here, so a naive walk would visit it twice; and `/opt` needs no skeleton list — FHS gives it none and Ubuntu ships it empty.
