Measured, and the answer is **yes — with three riders**, one of which is an article change.

The empty-folder rule does the heavy lifting: every stock directory that worried me is empty, so it prunes itself.

| Path | Owned? | Contents | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `share/{ca-certificates,fonts,man,texmf}` | no | empty | pruned |
| `share/{sgml,xml}` | no | only empty subdirs | pruned |
| `lib/python3.12/dist-packages` | no | empty | pruned |
| `bin/{talosctl,yq,flux,…}` | no | files | **findings** |
| `/usr/local/Brother`, `/opt/{az,google,Falco,brother}` | yes | — | not findings |

So on this machine your rule yields exactly the hand-installed software and nothing else.

**Rider 1 — report the topmost unowned path and stop there.** Otherwise `/usr/local/pycharm` arrives as several thousand findings instead of one. Recursion has to stop at what it reports.

**Rider 2 — prune at an owned directory, or the walk is enormous.** `/opt` is 30,178 paths here and 29,760 of them are `azure-cli`'s `/opt/az`. Deciding "everything below is dpkg-known" by walking it means listing and querying all of them on every run. Pruning at a directory a package owns — *except* the FHS skeleton dirs, which stay open because `/usr/local/bin` is owned by `cnpg` yet holds four unowned binaries — brings it back to about 50 paths. The trade: a file hand-dropped inside `/opt/google` would go unseen. I'd take that trade; say if you wouldn't.

**Rider 3 — `PKG-FR-MANUAL-SCOPE` has to change.** It currently requires a scan "shallow enough to name findings rather than walk either tree". Recursion is walking the tree, so the article's wording is the thing that has to move, not the code. With riders 1 and 2 the walk stays cheap, but it is a walk.

Agreed on the `/usr/local/man` symlink: not followed, so `share/man` isn't visited twice.

Waiting for your go — and for rider 2, if you'd rather not lose a file dropped inside an owned `/opt` package.

Rider 1: ok
Rider 2: good idea, but not good enough: /opt/google is too generic: currently we only have chrome there, but there can be other Google apps. Pruning/descending should be more intelligent.
Rider 3: with rider 2, rider 3 is not a problem: it is a walk, but shallow, so we conform to the article

Propose something for rider 2

Here's my proposal for rider 2 — the `/opt/az` vs `/opt/google` distinction is a *depth* question, not an ownership question, and FHS already fixes the depth.

## The rule

**Look for findings at depth 1 and depth 2 below each root, and no deeper.** At each level, batch one `dpkg --search` over the entries found.

- An entry a package owns is never a finding.
- An entry nobody owns is a finding, reported at the topmost level it appears (rider 1), not descended into.
- An unowned directory containing no file anywhere beneath it is ignored — one `find -type f -print -quit`, which stops at the first hit.
- `/usr/local`'s FHS skeleton names (`bin`, `etc`, `games`, `include`, `lib`, `man`, `sbin`, `share`, `src`) are never findings themselves, whoever owns them. `/opt` has no skeleton. `man` is a symlink and isn't followed.

## Why depth 2 is the right cut

FHS specifies `/opt/<provider>/<package>` — a vendor directory holding several products is exactly the layout it sanctions, so depth 2 is where a second Google app would appear, and it is where the standard stops nesting. Same for `/usr/local/<skeleton>/<thing>`.

Against your cases:

| Path | Depth | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/opt/az` (azure-cli) | 1 | owned → not a finding |
| `/opt/az/{bin,lib}` | 2 | owned → not findings; **stop** — the other 29,758 paths are never listed |
| `/opt/google` (chrome) | 1 | owned → not a finding |
| `/opt/google/chrome` | 2 | owned → nothing |
| `/opt/google/earth` (hypothetical, hand-installed) | 2 | **finding** ✓ |
| `/usr/local/bin` | 1 | skeleton → never a finding |
| `/usr/local/bin/talosctl` | 2 | unowned file → **finding** |
| `/usr/local/pycharm` | 1 | unowned, holds files → **finding**, not descended |
| `/usr/local/share/{sgml,xml}` | 2 | unowned, no files beneath → ignored |

Cost on this machine: about 17 directory listings and ~60 paths through one batched `dpkg --search`, against 30,178 for a full walk.

## The one thing it gives up

A file hand-dropped at depth 3 or deeper inside a package's own tree — `/opt/az/bin/mytool` — is not seen. Depth 2 is what makes the walk shallow, which is what keeps `PKG-FR-MANUAL-SCOPE` honest as you say in rider 3.

Two smaller notes: the skeleton list stays, because on a stock machine nobody owns `/usr/local/bin` and without the list it would be reported wholesale — that is the exact G28 bug. And it applies only at depth 1 under `/usr/local`, so it is nine stable FHS names, not a growing distro list.

You're right, and it's worse than the list: `share/zsh/site-functions` is a container three levels down, so both the nine names *and* the depth-2 cut fail for `/usr/local`.

The distribution already knows which directories are containers. **A directory under `/usr/local` is a container exactly when its counterpart outside `/usr/local` exists and dpkg owns it.** Measured here:

| `/usr/local/…` | counterpart | dpkg |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `share` | `/usr/share` | owned by 4 |
| `share/zsh` | `/usr/share/zsh` | owned by 23 |
| `share/zsh/site-functions` | `/usr/share/zsh/site-functions` | owned by 5 |
| `share/{sgml,xml}` | `/usr/share/{sgml,xml}` | owned by 5 / 7 |
| `bin`, `lib`, `include`, `src`, `games` | `/usr/…` | all owned |
| `pycharm` | `/usr/pycharm` | **absent** |

So your case resolves correctly with no list at all: `share` → `zsh` → `site-functions` are each containers, we walk through them, and `_task` is an unowned file — **the finding is `_task`, not the folder**. `/usr/local/pycharm` has no counterpart, so it stays a single finding and we don't descend into it.

**Proposed rule**

- `/opt`: depth 2, as agreed.
- `/usr/local`: descend while the counterpart exists and is dpkg-owned; report the first unowned thing that isn't a container; ignore anything with no file beneath it.
- No hardcoded skeleton list. It drops out — every FHS name is a container by this test, and so is every convention the distribution actually uses.

**Two exceptions and one soft spot, all measured**

- `/usr/etc` and `/usr/man` don't exist. `/usr/local/man` is a symlink we already skip; `/usr/local/etc` mirrors `/etc`, not `/usr/etc`, so it needs that one mapping.
- `/usr/lib/python3.12/dist-packages` doesn't exist (Debian uses `/usr/lib/python3/dist-packages`), so a pip-installed tree under `/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages` would be reported as that directory rather than as its contents. Coarse, but it flags rather than hides, and it's empty on this machine.
- I'd add a depth cap of 6 as a backstop against a pathological mirrored tree. The chain terminates on its own at 3–4 in practice.

Cost stays one batched `dpkg --search` per level, a handful of levels.

Yes — and it's better than both my proposals. The Ubuntu skeleton is created by **maintainer scripts**, which is exactly why dpkg doesn't own those directories. Grepping the installed packages' `postinst`/`preinst` for `/usr/local/...` on this machine yields it in full:

```
bin  etc  games  include  lib  sbin  share  src  man(symlink)      ← base-files
share/{ca-certificates, fonts, man, texmf}                          ← ca-certificates, fontconfig, tex-common
share/sgml + 5 subdirs, share/xml + 4 subdirs                       ← sgml-base, xml-core
lib/python3.12, lib/python3.12/dist-packages                        ← python3.12-minimal
share/i18n/SUPPORTED                                                ← locales
```

Every noise case we found is in there, including `lib/python3.12/dist-packages` — the one my `/usr` mirror missed. And it's self-maintaining: install a package that claims a directory under `/usr/local` and it declares itself.

**The rule**

A path under `/usr/local` or `/opt` is **not** a finding when any of these holds, and we descend through it:

1. dpkg owns it (file list), or
2. an installed package's maintainer script declares it (the grep above), or
3. it is a directory with no file anywhere beneath it.

Anything else unowned is a finding, reported topmost and not descended into. `/opt` keeps depth 2; `/usr/local` needs no depth limit because the container set now terminates on its own.

**Your zsh case, honestly:** `/usr/local/share/zsh` is not in the declared set, so if `_task` were hand-installed the *folder* would be reported. I'd argue that is now the right answer rather than a wart — no package created that folder, so it exists only because the user put something there. On this machine it doesn't arise: `task` owns it through its file list.

**Two caveats.** It's text extraction from shell scripts, so a path in a comment or a `PATH=` string would suppress a finding — it can only ever hide, never invent, and the risk is small. And it picks up file paths too (`/usr/local/bin/code` from `code.postinst`, `/usr/local/Brother/sane/…` from `brscan3.postinst`), which is correct: those are package-managed, not hand-installed.

Cost: one grep over `/var/lib/dpkg/info/*.{postinst,preinst}` on the source machine, plus the batched `dpkg --search` per level.

Waiting for your go.
I don't understand. What are pkg maintainer scripts? How are they the solution?

A `.deb` contains two things: the files it installs, and a few small shell scripts dpkg runs around installing it. The scripts are called `preinst`, `postinst`, `prerm`, `postrm` — "maintainer scripts", because the package's maintainer writes them. They're stored unpacked on the machine, one per package, in `/var/lib/dpkg/info/`.

Why that matters here: **dpkg only records the files a package ships.** That's what `dpkg --search` answers from. Anything a script *creates at install time* is invisible to it.

And Debian policy reserves `/usr/local` for the local administrator — a package isn't allowed to ship files into it. So the only way the distribution can put `/usr/local/bin` on your machine is to have a script create it. That is precisely why every one of those directories came back "no path found" when I searched dpkg for it: they exist, but they were made by a script, not shipped.

Here is that happening, verbatim from `/var/lib/dpkg/info/base-files.postinst` on this machine:

```
install_local_dir /usr/local
install_local_dir /usr/local/share
install_local_dir /usr/local/share/man
install_local_dir /usr/local/bin
install_local_dir /usr/local/games
install_local_dir /usr/local/lib
install_local_dir /usr/local/include
install_local_dir /usr/local/sbin
install_local_dir /usr/local/src
install_local_dir /usr/local/etc
ln -sf share/man "$DPKG_ROOT/usr/local/man"
```

Twelve other packages do the same for their own directories — `ca-certificates` makes `share/ca-certificates`, `xml-core` makes `share/xml`, `python3.12-minimal` makes `lib/python3.12/dist-packages`, and so on.

So the answer to "does Ubuntu have a fuller skeleton than FHS, can we use it?" is: yes, and **the scripts are the only place it is written down**. Reading them tells us which directories under `/usr/local` exist because the distribution put them there — which is exactly the set we must walk through rather than report. Everything else under `/usr/local` exists because a human put it there, which is what this scan is looking for.

Concretely, at scan time we'd grep those scripts once for `/usr/local/...` paths and treat the result as "not a finding, but keep looking inside".

**What kind of solution this is:** reading other packages' shell scripts as data. It's authoritative in the sense that nothing else states the list, and self-maintaining in that installing a package updates it. But it is text extraction from scripts, not an interface anyone promises to keep stable. If that's too clever for your taste, the honest alternative is a list we write and maintain ourselves in the repo — smaller and more predictable, at the cost of going stale when Ubuntu adds a directory.

"That is precisely why every one of those directories came back "no path found" when I searched dpkg": not true:
$ dpkg -S /usr/local/bin
cnpg: /usr/local/bin

You're right, and my sentence was wrong. Two of the nine are owned on this machine — `bin` by `cnpg` and `share` by `task` — and I'd measured exactly that myself earlier, then overstated it. The other seven (`etc`, `games`, `include`, `lib`, `man`, `sbin`, `src`) came back "no path found".

The accurate version: those two are owned because `cnpg` and `task` are third-party `.deb`s that **ship files into `/usr/local`**, which Debian policy tells archive packages not to do. Ubuntu's own `base-files` doesn't — it creates the directories from its script — so on a machine without such third-party packages all nine would be unowned.

That cuts in favour of the proposal rather than against it. # Package sync rework — the rulings and the work they imply

Decisions taken with the user. Each one changes the requirements first; the specification, the job guide, the code and the tests follow from there. Where a ruling contradicts an article, the article is what moves.

## Rulings

### A snap's revision is not a standing preference

A revision or channel difference stays a reviewed item, worded as the effect it has — "will overwrite revision X on <target> with revision Y" — and offers **apply and skip-once only**. It MUST NOT be markable machine-specific: nobody holds a revision as a per-machine preference, and the mark left the two machines' manifests disagreeing about a snap neither would raise again.

### A block replicates like a pin, not like a decision

An apt hold and a flatpak mask are **derived**: they follow the software they apply to, replicate without review, and are never items. This is `PKG-FR-PIN-ALWAYS`'s treatment of pins, for the same reason — a block changes nothing about what software exists, only about what may move, and replicating one costs nothing.

Consequences: the merged-question machinery, the block-state decision store, and every article and row that makes a block separately decidable go. Sweep all of section B, E.8, F.13 and N4–N6, and every row citing `PKG-FR-BLOCKS-REPLICATE`, `PKG-FR-APT-HOLD-*`, `PKG-FR-SNAP-HOLD` or `PKG-FR-FLATPAK-MASK` — B14 among them, not only the rows named here.

### A hold whose package is absent is a bookkeeping failure

On either machine. The run aborts and tells the user to clean it up. This is not a principle about bookkeeping in general; it is a decision not to carry logic for a case that should not exist.

### A flatpak filter is in force before the applications install

Order: add or sync the remote, add or sync its filter, then install. Nothing is cleared first, so no window exists in which the target's remote offers more than either machine meant. A filter that denies an application the source itself has installed is a bookkeeping failure of the same kind — abort and say so. A filter that cannot be written or applied warns, naming the filter and the remote.

### A remote's trust travels wherever it is stored

`PKG-FR-FLATPAK-REMOTE-TRUST` has no exception. A key held through the ostree per-remote `gpgkeypath` option is read and carried like any other.

### Collateral the user was never asked about

D37: a removal candidate the user skipped, carried off by another approved removal's cascade, must be **asked** about, not refused at the guard. The cost — one `apt-get --dry-run` per candidate on a run with removals — is accepted.

### Software no manager can reproduce is found by diffing, not by scanning one machine

`manual_installs_sync` scans **both** machines and presents what the target lacks. A finding that the target already holds is not raised, which is what makes a secondary path — a symlink in `bin` pointing at an app in `/opt` — stop being asked about once the snippet has run. Resolution is still decided by the **source's** registry alone: it is the one in charge, and it reaches the target in the same run or the run aborts.

### Where hand-installed software lives

Scanned: `/opt`, and directly under `/usr/local` — plus inside `bin`, `sbin`, `lib`, `games`, `src`. Never scanned: `etc`, `include`, `man`, `share`. Anything installed there is assumed to arrive with an application the scan finds elsewhere.

A finding may be a file, a directory or a symlink. It is not a finding if dpkg owns it, if it is one of the directories `base-files.postinst` creates, or if it is a directory with no file anywhere beneath it.

Under `/opt`, an unowned entry is judged by its own shape:

| `/opt/<X>` holds | Meaning | Action |
| - | - | - |
| files | `/opt/<app>` | `<X>` is the finding |
| no files, one directory | `/opt/<vendor>/<app>` | that directory is the finding |
| no files, several directories | cannot be told apart | ask the user which it is |
| nothing | — | not a finding |

The FHS skeleton list is nine names from `base-files.postinst`, held as a constant with a VM test asserting the machine still declares exactly those.

## The work

1. Snap revision: apply/skip-once, no mark
2. Apt holds derived, like pins
3. Flatpak masks derived, like pins
4. Hold without package: abort, name it
5. Flatpak order: remote, filter, install
6. Filter failure warns, never clears first
7. Read remote key from `gpgkeypath`
8. D37: ask about the skipped candidate
9. New scan scope, six `/usr/local` dirs
10. `/opt` vendor-or-app question when ambiguous
11. Diff-based: scan both machines
12. Source registry alone decides resolution
13. Delete the invented 25-finding limit
14. Rename "ratchet" to plain wording
15. Sweep untagged tests, correct marks
16. D61, F121, H133 become U
17. Delete J107 row
18. Close K89, do K67 properly
19. Drop K82, K88 gap entries
20. Integration tests for collateral damage
21. Integration tests for apt origins
22. Re-audit V rows, drop unit-provable
23. Five checks, push, watch CI

Items 9–13 depend on 11's shape. Items 14–19 land after everything that moves a row.

## Two standing rules this settles

**A test tier follows what is under test.** A branch a unit test proves reliably needs no integration test. Integration is for what depends on real package-manager or machine behaviour, and nothing else.

**"Ratchet" is not this project's word.** The cross-reference between the scenario document and the suite is called what it is.
